idiom_name: ArcSwap<RoutingTable> (arc-swap) with a HashMap lookup and one snapshot per message
implementation_notes: Rust's ownership rules push the runtime-editable rule base into an immutable snapshot behind an atomic pointer: ArcSwap<RoutingTable> gives lock-free reads of a consistent table while a control task builds a new RoutingTable and swaps it with store; with the standard library only, RwLock<Arc<RoutingTable>> is the fallback, at the cost of locking and a per-read clone of the Arc. Each message loads the guard once so it is routed entirely by one generation, and the guard keeps the old table alive until the message finishes - exactly the lifetime the borrow checker would otherwise force you to hand-manage. Routing logic itself is a match on the message enum plus a HashMap lookup; for an HTTP-shaped router, axum's Router can be rebuilt and swapped the same way.
pitfalls: RwLock<Arc<T>> needs an Arc clone per read and still exposes lock contention, while ArcSwap does not; mixing both idioms in one router makes the guard lifetimes confusing.
Holding a read guard across an await point keeps an old table alive longer than intended (and a std RwLock guard is not Send at all).
A publish that tries to mutate the published table in place - through Arc::get_mut or while a guard is held - fails or blocks; always build the new table off to the side and store it.
